presentingComplaint: Found drowsy and confused, then had a witnessed generalised seizure; brought in stuporous
history: Type 2 diabetic and hypertensive man with CKD stage 3b (baseline creatinine 2.1 mg/dL) known to nephrology. Over the preceding 8-10 days his family noted progressively reduced urine output, worsening fatigue, poor appetite with intermittent vomiting, hiccups and increasing daytime somnolence. On the morning of admission he was noted to be confused and disoriented at home, twitching in both arms, and then had a single witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting ~90 seconds followed by post-ictal stupor. He had recently been started on a high-dose NSAID by a local practitioner for back pain and had been eating and drinking poorly. No head trauma, no fever, no headache preceding the event, no neck stiffness, no known liver disease and no alcohol use. Not yet on dialysis. This is a severe, critical presentation - the abrupt seizure and depressed consciousness raise concern for a primary CNS catastrophe, but the trajectory and biochemistry point to a diffuse metabolic cause.
examination: Stuporous, GCS 9 (E2 V2 M5), opens eyes to pain, no meaningful speech, localises. Uraemic fetor noted. No neck stiffness, Kernig/Brudzinski negative. Pupils equal and reactive; no gaze deviation, no lateralising motor deficit, plantars equivocal bilaterally. Prominent multifocal myoclonus and bilateral asterixis when limbs are held extended. Mild bilateral pitting pedal oedema, dry oral mucosa with reduced skin turgor. No papilloedema on fundoscopy. Chest clear, abdomen soft with no organomegaly and no ascites, no flap-associated jaundice or spider naevi.
imaging: Non-contrast CT head: no haemorrhage, no mass, no midline shift, no acute infarct, no cerebral oedema. Chest X-ray: mild pulmonary congestion, no consolidation. Renal ultrasound: bilateral echogenic kidneys ~9 cm with no hydronephrosis (chronic parenchymal disease on a background of acute-on-chronic injury).
microbiology: Blood cultures sent and negative at 48h. CSF (after platelet check): opening pressure normal, 2 cells/µL, protein 0.4 g/L, glucose normal, Gram stain negative, meningoencephalitis PCR panel negative - excluding CNS infection.
differentialDiagnoses: Uraemic (metabolic) encephalopathy from acute-on-chronic kidney injury - leading diagnosis
Intracerebral haemorrhage / structural CNS lesion (excluded on CT)
CNS infection: meningitis / encephalitis (excluded on CSF)
Hyponatraemic encephalopathy (mild hyponatraemia contributory but insufficient alone)
Hepatic encephalopathy (no liver disease, normal ammonia and INR)
finalDiagnosis: Severe metabolic (uraemic) encephalopathy due to NSAID-precipitated acute-on-chronic kidney injury, with multifactorial metabolic derangement (uraemia, high anion-gap metabolic acidosis, hyperkalaemia, hypocalcaemia, mild hyponatraemia) producing seizure, myoclonus, asterixis and depressed consciousness
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Coma and Metabolic Encephalopathies
KDIGO - Acute Kidney Injury Clinical Practice Guideline - 2012
contraindications: Avoid nephrotoxins and iodinated contrast; stop the offending NSAID immediately
Avoid renally-cleared sedatives / long-acting benzodiazepines outside active seizure control as they deepen encephalopathy
Avoid gadolinium in this eGFR range (nephrogenic systemic fibrosis risk)
edgeCases: Diffuse metabolic encephalopathy can cause seizures and multifocal myoclonus that mimic a primary neurological catastrophe - a normal CT and CSF are decisive
If ammonia were elevated with cirrhotic stigmata the picture would shift toward hepatic encephalopathy
Hyperkalaemia with metabolic acidosis and uraemic pericarditis/oliguria are urgent indications for renal replacement therapy
Symmetrical asterixis and myoclonus without focal deficit strongly favour a metabolic over a structural cause
expectedMaiK: Recognise severe metabolic (uraemic) encephalopathy: exclude structural and infective CNS causes (normal CT and CSF), correct life-threatening derangements (hyperkalaemia, acidosis), and arrange urgent renal replacement therapy for the uraemic encephalopathy and refractory metabolic disturbance.
expectedNextQuestions: What is the baseline renal function and is he already established on dialysis?
What nephrotoxic or CNS-active drugs (NSAIDs, opioids, sedatives) has he taken recently?
What is the trend in urine output and fluid balance?
Are there uraemic complications (pericardial rub, resistant hyperkalaemia, acidosis) mandating emergent dialysis?
Any history of liver disease, alcohol use or features to suggest hepatic encephalopathy instead?
expectedInvestigations: Urgent renal profile with urea, creatinine and eGFR
Serum electrolytes including potassium, calcium, phosphate and venous blood gas for anion gap
Serum ammonia, LFTs and INR to exclude hepatic encephalopathy
Non-contrast CT head to exclude haemorrhage/structural lesion
Lumbar puncture with CSF analysis to exclude CNS infection
Capillary glucose and TSH to exclude hypoglycaemia and myxoedema
ECG for hyperkalaemic changes; renal ultrasound for obstruction/chronicity
regressionAssertions: Engine ranks metabolic_enceph as the top diagnosis
Engine does NOT classify this as a primary CNS infection or structural haemorrhage given normal CT and CSF
Engine flags severe uraemia with hyperkalaemia and acidosis as an indication for urgent renal replacement therapy
Focal-deficit-driven stroke pathway is not triggered (asterixis/myoclonus without lateralising signs)
